comments.author: @Cyb-t8u
comments.text:
The Indigenous Taíno people laid the foundation for jerk cooking in Jamaica.
While it is spelled "jerk" (likely derived from the Spanish word charqui, meaning dried meat). What we know today as Jamaican jerk is a brilliant culinary fusion born from resilience:
Long before Europeans arrived, the Taíno people preserved and slow-cooked wild meat using native allspice (pimento) wood, salt, and peppers on wooden racks called barbacoa (the root of the word barbecue).
• The Maroon Innovation: In the 17th century, escaped enslaved Africans (the Maroons) fled into the Blue Mountains and integrated with the surviving Taíno. To avoid detection by British soldiers, the Maroons adapted the Taíno style by cooking meat in smokeless underground pits and adding intense African spices, including Scotch bonnet peppers.
Today, this ancient tradition remains Jamaica's most iconic flavor.

replies.text: Understandable after Florida! Jamaica's are American crocodiles, the same species found in South Florida, and they're generally shy — they keep to quiet river mouths and mangroves like the Black River, and attacks on people are rare. Still, best admired from a boat!

replies.author: @PlanetVista4K
replies.text: They've been there all along — American crocodiles are native to Jamaica's coastal wetlands, especially around the Black River in St. Elizabeth, and they've been protected since 1971. There's even one sitting on top of the national coat of arms.
